10.1002_inf2.70183: Various carbon frameworks are central to rechargeable‐ion batteries, while continuous structural and compositional regulation provides broad opportunities to improve fast‐charging capability, storage capacity, and cycling stability. However, a unified chemistry‐based understanding that directly connects carbon structure with electrochemical behavior remains insufficient. Herein, bonding chemistry is proposed as an atom‐level framework for interpreting diverse carbon materials. It encompasses intrinsic C/C hybridization, carbon‐heteroatom interactions, and dynamic bonding between carbon frameworks and charge‐carrying species during electrochemical storage. From this perspective, carbon materials are re‐examined according to their hybridization‐derived frameworks, porous textures, defect‐related features, and corresponding electrochemical consequences. Carbon‐nonmetal covalent configurations, polarized carbon‐halogen bonds, and metal‐carbon or heteroatom‐mediated coordination environments are further analyzed in terms of bond type, polarity, strength, orbital coupling, spatial distribution, and dynamic evolution. The bonding changes associated with ion adsorption, insertion, co‐intercalation, and conversion reactions are also discussed. Overall, this perspective establishes a cross‐scale, bond‐descriptor‐based framework that links synthetic regulation to local bonding states and subsequently to ion‐storage thermodynamics, transport kinetics, interfacial chemistry, and reaction reversibility, thereby enabling a more systematic and predictive design of advanced carbon frameworks for rechargeable‐ion batteries. image
10.1002_smll.202512729: As the efficiency of perovskite solar cells (PSCs) continues to rise, extending their operational stability outdoors has become critical for commercial adoption. However, in outdoor high‐energy ultraviolet (UV) and strong oxidizing environments, it is easy to cause lattice distortion of perovskite and accelerate the aging of photovoltaic modules. Herein, to address UV‐induced lattice distortion and oxidation in perovskite layers, we introduce natural grape seed proanthocyanidin (OPC) at the TiO 2 /perovskite buried interface. OPC, which serves as a bridge, forms a stable interface bonding network through hydrogen bonding between its multiple phenolic hydroxyl groups, and the TiO 2 surface is covered with hydroxyl groups (─OH), reducing the density of defect states on the ETL surface, suppressing carrier recombination, and thereby improving carrier mobility and extraction efficiency. Meanwhile, the C═C and ─OH functional groups of OPC molecules bind with undercoordinated Pb 2+ ions to inhibit nonradiative recombination, promote the perovskite crystal growth, and form excellent perovskite films. With the OPC “antioxidation‐passivation‐UV protection” trinity buried interface engineering strategy, the PCE of the ingeniously designed PSCs upgraded from 22.91% to 24.79%. In addition, the modification of OPC effectively blocks the erosion of the perovskite crystal phase by ultraviolet radiation, providing excellent UV/oxidation resistance stability.
10.1016_j.envpol.2025.127396: Coastal deltas are increasingly exposed to microplastic (MP) pollution due to complex interactions among hydrological dynamics, land use change and anthropogenic pressures. While marine MP contamination is widely studied, their fate and transport in deltaic floodplains-particularly inland soils-remain poorly understood. This review synthesizes empirical evidence from 76 peer-reviewed studies to assess MP distribution in deltaic environments and identify critical knowledge gaps. Evidence reveals consistent MP presence across diverse deltas, with highest concentrations often found in low-energy zones influenced by flooding, proximity to urban areas, and agricultural activity. MPs commonly appear as fibres and fragments, and are frequently associated with metals and other co-contaminants. Despite this growing body of research, there is a notable absence of mechanistic models that explain how MPs are transported, deposited, and remobilized across deltaic floodplains. To address this, we propose a conceptual model capturing the cyclical deposition, contaminant enrichment and remobilization of MPs in floodplains. The Bengal Delta is highlighted as a representative system illustrating how large, densely populated catchments intensify MP fluxes. This review emphasizes the need for integrated modelling and monitoring approaches that consider delta-specific drivers. Closing these knowledge gaps is essential to predict long-term impacts and to develop effective mitigation policies for vulnerable and ecologically important deltaic environments.
10.1016_j.seppur.2026.136910: Chemical absorption using amine-based solvents is among the most mature technologies that can be im-plemented for CO2 capture. However, its widespread deployment is hindered by design constraints and exces-sive costs. Recent improvements to chemical absorption include usage of hollow fiber membrane (HFM) con-tactors as an alternative gas-liquid contactor for chemical absorption instead of packed columns; In addition, microwave (MW) heating was recently tested as a heat source to regenerate spent alkanolamine solvents.This work aims to study the combining of HFM and MW technologies by examining the interactions of the electromagnetic fields, and the mass and heat transfers phenomena taking place during desorption of CO2 from aqueous ethanolamine solvent in a HFM. To this end, an experimental study was carried out in Part-I, investi-gating a single hollow fiber placed inside a mono-mode MW applicator. The solvent was made to circulate on the lumen side of the fiber while traversing the applicator where it absorbs MW energy. Experimental desorption fluxes were measured at steady state regime with varying carbonation ratio, tem-perature, solvent and sweeping gas flow rates. Results were found in the same order of magnitude as those reported in literature where membrane modules were operated isothermally under atmospheric or vacuum pressures. Similar performances point in the direction of discrediting the speculated non-thermal effects that microwaves might have on the desorption reaction kinetics as suggested in literature. This work is completed with Part-II dealing with the development of a numerical model describing the tested HFC-MW desorption system.
10.1021_acsami.5c17045: Growing demand for high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) has established high-nickel layered oxides as one of the most promising cathode candidates. Compared with commonly used high-nickel polycrystalline layered oxides, high-nickel single-crystalline layered oxides have attracted more attention due to their improved structural and cycling stability. However, the synthesis of high-nickel single-crystalline nickel cobalt manganese lithium oxide (NCM) particles requires a high calcination temperature, leading to particle agglomeration and aggravated Li + /Ni 2 + cation mixing. In addition, high-nickel single-crystalline NCM could suffer from sluggish Li + diffusion kinetics and structural degradation caused by severe phase transformation. Herein, we adopted the molten salt method to prepare a single-crystalline LiNi 0.95 Co 0.025 Mn 0.025 O 2 cathode at a relatively low synthesis temperature to relieve particle agglomeration. Meanwhile, the Nb doping strategy is employed to broaden the interplanar spacing to facilitate Li + diffusion, inhibit the Li + /Ni 2+ cation mixing, and restrain the severe phase transformation. The obtained Nb-doped single-crystalline LiNi 0.95 Co 0.025 Mn 0.025 O 2 (SC-NCM-N) cathode achieves a high reversible capacity of 216.4 mAh g –1 at 0.1 C (1 C = 180 mAh g –1 ), along with an improved capacity retention (88.7% after 100 cycles at 1 C) in comparison with the polycrystalline LiNi 0.95 Co 0.025 Mn 0.025 O 2 (P-NCM, 66.8%) and pristine single-crystalline LiNi 0.95 Co 0.025 Mn 0.025 O 2 (SC-NCM, 79.1%). This work offers insights into developing high-nickel single-crystalline cathodes for high-energy-density LIBs.
10.1039_d5ta10161a: Molecule-specific micropore engineering of biomass-derived activated carbons enables high quinone utilization and exceptional durability in aqueous all-organic batteries, achieving ∼17 Wh kg −1 and 99.75% capacity retention over 3000 cycles.
